questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A yogi's guru resides in a Karakoram cave, located $1000 \text{ km}$ away from the house of the yogi. The yogi asserts that whenever he thinks about his guru, the guru instantly knows about it. Determine the minimum possible time interval between the yogi thinking about the guru and the guru becoming aware of it.
questions.solution:
According to the special theory of relativity, no signal or information can travel faster than the speed of light in vacuum.

The maximum speed of information transfer is $c = 3 \times 10^8 \text{ m/s}$.

The distance between the yogi and the guru is $d = 1000 \text{ km} = 10^6 \text{ m}$.

The minimum possible time interval is the time taken by light to travel this distance.

$t = \dfrac{d}{c}$

$t = \dfrac{10^6}{3 \times 10^8} = \dfrac{1}{300} \text{ s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Measured at rest, a rod has an exact length of $1 \text{ m}$. Determine its length when it travels at a speed of $3 \times 10^5 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
The rest length of the rod is $L_0 = 1 \text{ m}$.

The speed of the rod is $v = 3 \times 10^5 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.

The speed of light is $c = 3 \times 10^8 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.

Using the length contraction formula:

$L = L_0 \sqrt{1 - \dfrac{v^2}{c^2}}$

Substituting the given values:

$L = 1 \times \sqrt{1 - \left(\dfrac{3 \times 10^5}{3 \times 10^8}\right)^2}$

$L = \sqrt{1 - (10^{-3})^2}$

$L = (1 - 10^{-6})^{1/2}$

Using the binomial approximation $(1 - x)^n \approx 1 - nx$ for $x \ll 1$:

$L \approx 1 - \dfrac{1}{2} \times 10^{-6}$

$L \approx 1 - 0.0000005$

$L = 0.9999995 \text{ m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Measured at rest, a rod has an exact length of $1 \text{ m}$. Determine its length when it travels at a speed of $3 \times 10^6 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
The rest length of the rod is $L_0 = 1 \text{ m}$.

The speed of the rod is $v = 3 \times 10^6 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.

The speed of light is $c = 3 \times 10^8 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.

According to the special theory of relativity, the contracted length $L$ is given by:

$L = L_0 \sqrt{1 - \dfrac{v^2}{c^2}}$

Substituting the given values:

$L = 1 \times \sqrt{1 - \left(\dfrac{3 \times 10^6}{3 \times 10^8}\right)^2}$

$L = \sqrt{1 - (10^{-2})^2}$

$L = \sqrt{1 - 10^{-4}}$

Using the binomial approximation $(1 - x)^{1/2} \approx 1 - \dfrac{x}{2}$ for $x \ll 1$:

$L \approx 1 - \dfrac{10^{-4}}{2}$

$L \approx 1 - 0.00005$

$L = 0.99995 \text{ m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Measured at rest, a rod has an exact length of $1 \text{ m}$. Determine its length when it travels at a speed of $3 \times 10^7 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
Given rest length of the rod, $L_0 = 1 \text{ m}$

Speed of the rod, $v = 3 \times 10^7 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

Speed of light, $c = 3 \times 10^8 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

Using the length contraction formula:

$L = L_0 \sqrt{1 - \dfrac{v^2}{c^2}}$

Substituting the given values:

$L = 1 \times \sqrt{1 - \left(\dfrac{3 \times 10^7}{3 \times 10^8}\right)^2}$

$L = \sqrt{1 - (0.1)^2}$

$L = \sqrt{1 - 0.01}$

$L = (1 - 0.01)^{1/2}$

Using the binomial approximation $(1 - x)^n \approx 1 - nx$ for $x \ll 1$:

$L \approx 1 - \dfrac{1}{2}(0.01)$

$L \approx 1 - 0.005 = 0.995 \text{ m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A shop owner measures a suitcase kept on a rack to be $50 \text{ cm} \times 25 \text{ cm} \times 10 \text{ cm}$. A traveller takes this suitcase on a train travelling with a velocity of $0.6c$. If the suitcase is oriented with its length parallel to the train's velocity, determine the dimensions measured by an observer on the ground.
questions.solution:
The proper dimensions of the suitcase are $L_0 = 50 \text{ cm}$, $W_0 = 25 \text{ cm}$, and $H_0 = 10 \text{ cm}$.

The train is moving with a velocity $v = 0.6c$. Length contraction occurs only along the direction of motion (parallel to the length).

The length measured by the observer on the ground is given by:

$L = L_0 \sqrt{1 - \dfrac{v^2}{c^2}}$

$L = 50 \sqrt{1 - (0.6)^2} = 50 \sqrt{1 - 0.36} = 50 \times 0.8 = 40 \text{ cm}$

The dimensions perpendicular to the direction of motion remain unchanged. Thus, the width and height are $25 \text{ cm}$ and $10 \text{ cm}$ respectively.

The dimensions measured by the observer on the ground are $40 \text{ cm} \times 25 \text{ cm} \times 10 \text{ cm}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A shop owner measures a suitcase kept on a rack to be $50 \text{ cm} \times 25 \text{ cm} \times 10 \text{ cm}$. A traveller takes this suitcase on a train travelling with a velocity of $0.6c$. If the suitcase is oriented with its length parallel to the train's velocity, determine the dimensions measured by the traveller.
questions.solution:
The proper dimensions of the suitcase are measured when it is at rest relative to the observer. The shop owner measures the proper dimensions as $50 \text{ cm} \times 25 \text{ cm} \times 10 \text{ cm}$.

When the traveller takes the suitcase on the train, both the traveller and the suitcase are in the same reference frame. The relative velocity between the traveller and the suitcase is zero.

Since there is no relative motion between them, the traveller does not observe any length contraction and measures the proper dimensions of the suitcase.

Therefore, the dimensions measured by the traveller remain $50 \text{ cm} \times 25 \text{ cm} \times 10 \text{ cm}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A person standing on a platform notes that a train travelling with a velocity of $0.6c$ requires one second to pass by them. Determine the length of the train as seen by this person.
questions.solution:
The velocity of the train is given as $v = 0.6c$.

Substituting the speed of light $c = 3 \times 10^8 \text{ m/s}$:

$v = 0.6 \times 3 \times 10^8 \text{ m/s} = 1.8 \times 10^8 \text{ m/s}$

The time taken for the train to pass the person on the platform is $t = 1 \text{ s}$.

The length of the train as observed by the person is simply the distance the train travels in their frame of reference during this time interval.

$L = v \times t$

$L = 1.8 \times 10^8 \text{ m/s} \times 1 \text{ s} = 1.8 \times 10^8 \text{ m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A person standing on a platform notes that a train travelling with a velocity of $0.6c$ requires one second to pass by them. Determine the rest length of the train.
questions.solution:
The velocity of the train is $v = 0.6c$ and the time taken to pass the observer is $t = 1 \text{ s}$.

The length of the train as measured by the observer on the platform is the contracted length $L$.

$L = v \times t = 0.6c \times 1 = 0.6 \times 3 \times 10^8 \text{ m} = 1.8 \times 10^8 \text{ m}$

According to the length contraction formula, the relation between the contracted length $L$ and the rest length $L_0$ is:

$L = L_0 \sqrt{1 - \dfrac{v^2}{c^2}}$

$L_0 = \dfrac{L}{\sqrt{1 - \dfrac{v^2}{c^2}}}$

Substituting the values of $L$ and $v$:

$L_0 = \dfrac{1.8 \times 10^8}{\sqrt{1 - (0.6)^2}}$

$L_0 = \dfrac{1.8 \times 10^8}{\sqrt{1 - 0.36}}$

$L_0 = \dfrac{1.8 \times 10^8}{0.8}$

$L_0 = 2.25 \times 10^8 \text{ m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An aeroplane flies over a rectangular field of dimensions $100 \text{ m} \times 50 \text{ m}$, moving parallel to its length. Determine the speed of the plane such that the field appears as a square in the plane's frame of reference.
questions.solution:
Let the proper length of the field be $L_0 = 100 \text{ m}$ and the proper width be $W_0 = 50 \text{ m}$.

The aeroplane moves parallel to the length of the field with speed $v$. According to the theory of relativity, the length of the field observed from the aeroplane undergoes length contraction, while the width remains unchanged.

The observed length is given by $L = L_0 \sqrt{1 - \dfrac{v^2}{c^2}}$.

The observed width is $W = W_0 = 50 \text{ m}$.

For the field to appear as a square in the aeroplane's frame of reference, the observed length must be equal to the observed width:

$L = W$

$100 \sqrt{1 - \dfrac{v^2}{c^2}} = 50$

$\sqrt{1 - \dfrac{v^2}{c^2}} = \dfrac{1}{2}$

Squaring both sides:

$1 - \dfrac{v^2}{c^2} = \dfrac{1}{4}$

$\dfrac{v^2}{c^2} = \dfrac{3}{4}$

$v = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} c$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The rest distance between Lucknow and Bhopal is $1000 \text{ km}$. A nonstop train travels at $360 \text{ km h}^{-1}$. Determine the distance between Lucknow and Bhopal in the train frame.
questions.solution:
The rest distance is $L_0 = 1000 \text{ km} = 10^6 \text{ m}$.

The speed of the train is $v = 360 \text{ km h}^{-1} = 360 \times \dfrac{5}{18} \text{ m s}^{-1} = 100 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.

According to the length contraction formula, the distance in the train's frame is $L = L_0 \sqrt{1 - \dfrac{v^2}{c^2}}$.

Since $v \ll c$, using the binomial expansion gives $L \approx L_0 \left(1 - $\dfrac{v^2}{2c^2}\right).

The decrease in length is $\Delta L = L_0 - L = $\dfrac{L_0 v^2}{2c^2}.

Substituting the values:

$\Delta L = $\dfrac{10^6 \times (100)^2}{2 \times (3 \times 10^8)^2}

$\Delta L = $\dfrac{10^{10}}{18 \times 10^{16}}

$\Delta L = $\dfrac{1}{18} \times$10^{-6} \text{ m}$

$\Delta L \approx 0.0555 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m} = 55.5 \text{ nm} \approx 56 \text{ nm}$

Thus, the distance in the train's frame is $56 \text{ nm}$ less than $1000 \text{ km}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The rest distance between Lucknow and Bhopal is $1000 \text{ km}$. A nonstop train travels at $360 \text{ km h}^{-1}$. Determine the amount of time that elapses in the train frame between Lucknow and Bhopal.
questions.solution:
\Delta t = \dfrac{L_0}{v} = \dfrac{10^6}{100} = 10^4 \text{ s}$

Converting this time into minutes:
$\Delta t = \dfrac{10000}{60} \text{ min} = \dfrac{500}{3} \text{ min}$

The time elapsed in the train frame is the proper time $\Delta t_0$, given by the time dilation formula:
$\Delta t_0 = \Delta t \sqrt{1 - \dfrac{v^2}{c^2}}$

The difference in time between the two frames is:
$\Delta t - \Delta t_0 = \Delta t \left($1 - $\sqrt{1 - \dfrac{v^2}{c^2}}\right)

Since $v \ll c$, using the binomial expansion $(1 - x)^{1/2} $\approx$1 - $\dfrac{x}{2}:
\Delta$t - $\Delta$t_0 $\approx \Delta$t \left(\dfrac{v^2}{2c^2}\right)$

Substituting the given values ($c = 3 \times 10^8 \text{ m s}^{-1}$):
$\Delta t - \Delta t_0 = 10^4 \times \dfrac{(100)^2}{2 \times (3 \times 10^8)^2}$

$\Delta t - \Delta t_0 = 10^4 \times \dfrac{10^4}{18 \times 10^{16}}$

$\Delta t - \Delta t_0 = \dfrac{1}{18 \times 10^8} \text{ s}$

$\Delta t - \Delta t_0 = \dfrac{10}{18} \times 10^{-9} \text{ s} = \dfrac{5}{9} \text{ ns} \approx 0.56 \text{ ns}$

Thus, the time elapsed in the train frame is $0.56 \text{ ns}$ less than $\dfrac{500}{3} \text{ min}$.$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A person travels by a car at a speed of $180 \text{ km h}^{-1}$. By his wristwatch, the journey from station $X$ to station $Y$ takes exactly $10 \text{ hours}$. What is the rest distance between the two stations?
questions.solution:
Speed of the car, $v = 180 \text{ km h}^{-1} = 180 \times \dfrac{5}{18} \text{ m s}^{-1} = 50 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.

Time measured by the wristwatch of the person in the car is the proper time, $\Delta t_0 = 10 \text{ h}$.

Distance measured in the car's frame is $L = v \Delta t_0 = 180 \text{ km h}^{-1} \times 10 \text{ h} = 1800 \text{ km}$.

The rest distance between the two stations is the proper length $L_0$. In the car's frame, the distance between the stations appears contracted, so $L = L_0 \sqrt{1 - \dfrac{v^2}{c^2}}$.

Therefore, $L_0 = \dfrac{L}{\sqrt{1 - \dfrac{v^2}{c^2}}}$.

Using the binomial expansion for $v \ll c$:

$L_0 \approx L \left(1 + \dfrac{v^2}{2c^2}\right) = L + \dfrac{L v^2}{2c^2}$

The additional distance is $\Delta L = \dfrac{L v^2}{2c^2}$.

Substituting the values $L = 1800 \text{ km} = 1.8 \times 10^6 \text{ m}$ and $c = 3 \times 10^8 \text{ m s}^{-1}$:

$\Delta L = \dfrac{1.8 \times 10^6 \times (50)^2}{2 \times (3 \times 10^8)^2}$

$\Delta L = \dfrac{1.8 \times 10^6 \times 2500}{18 \times 10^{16}} = 25 \times 10^{-9} \text{ m} = 25 \text{ nm}$

Thus, the rest distance is $25 \text{ nm}$ more than $1800 \text{ km}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A person travels by a car at a speed of $180 \text{ km h}^{-1}$. By his wristwatch, the journey from station $X$ to station $Y$ takes exactly $10 \text{ hours}$. How much time is taken in the road frame by the car to go from station $X$ to station $Y$?
questions.solution:
The proper time measured by the wristwatch in the car is $\Delta \tau = 10 \text{ hours} = 36000 \text{ s}$.

The speed of the car is $v = 180 \text{ km h}^{-1} = 180 \times \dfrac{5}{18} \text{ m s}^{-1} = 50 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.

The time measured in the road frame is $\Delta t$. According to the time dilation formula:

$\Delta t = \dfrac{\Delta \tau}{\sqrt{1 - \dfrac{v^2}{c^2}}}$

Since $v \ll c$, we can use the binomial approximation $(1 - x)^{-1/2} \approx 1 + \dfrac{x}{2}$:

$\Delta t \approx \Delta \tau \left(1 + $\dfrac{v^2}{2c^2}\right)

The extra time taken in the road frame is:

$\Delta t - \Delta \tau = \Delta \tau $\dfrac{v^2}{2c^2}

Substituting the values:

$\Delta t - \Delta \tau = 36000 \times $\dfrac{1}{2} \times \left(\dfrac{50}{3 \times 10^8}\right)^2$

$\Delta t - \Delta \tau = 18000 \times $\dfrac{2500}{9 \times 10^{16}}

$\Delta t - \Delta \tau = 2000 \times $\dfrac{2500}{10^{16}}

$\Delta t - \Delta \tau = $\dfrac{5 \times 10^6}{10^{16}} =$5 \times 10^{-10} \text{ s}$

$\Delta t - \Delta \tau = 0.5 \times 10^{-9} \text{ s} = 0.5 \text{ ns}$

Therefore, the time taken in the road frame is $0.5 \text{ ns}$ more than $10 \text{ hours}.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A person is travelling on a spaceship that moves at a speed of $5c/13$. Determine the time interval calculated by this person between consecutive birthday celebrations of his friend on the earth.
questions.solution:
The proper time interval between consecutive birthdays on Earth is $\Delta t_0 = 1 \text{ year}$.

The speed of the spaceship is $v = \dfrac{5c}{13}$.

The time interval measured by the person on the spaceship is given by the time dilation formula:

$\Delta t = \dfrac{\Delta t_0}{\sqrt{1 - \dfrac{v^2}{c^2}}}$

Substituting the given values:

$\Delta t = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - \left(\dfrac{5}{13}\right)^2}}$

$\Delta t = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - \dfrac{25}{169}}}$

$\Delta t = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\dfrac{144}{169}}}$

$\Delta t = \dfrac{13}{12} \text{ year}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A person is travelling on a spaceship that moves at a speed of $5c/13$. Determine the time interval calculated by his friend on the earth between consecutive birthday celebrations of the person on the spaceship.
questions.solution:
The proper time interval between consecutive birthday celebrations for the person on the spaceship is $\Delta t_0 = 1 \text{ year}$.

The speed of the spaceship is $v = \dfrac{5c}{13}$.

The time interval measured by the friend on Earth is given by the time dilation formula:

$\Delta t = \dfrac{\Delta t_0}{\sqrt{1 - \dfrac{v^2}{c^2}}}$

Substituting the given values:

$\Delta t = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - \left(\dfrac{5}{13}\right)^2}}$

$\Delta t = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - \dfrac{25}{169}}}$

$\Delta t = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\dfrac{144}{169}}}$

$\Delta t = \dfrac{1}{\dfrac{12}{13}} = \dfrac{13}{12} \text{ year}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: According to the station clocks, two babies are born at the exact same instant, one in Kanpur and the other in Agra. Who is elder in the reference frame of the 12033 Shatabdi Express travelling from Kanpur to Agra?
options: Both babies are of the exact same age
It depends on the exact speed of the train
questions.solution:
Let the ground frame be $S$ and the train frame be $S'$.

Let Kanpur be at the origin $x = 0$ and Agra be at $x = L$, where $L > 0$.

The train moves from Kanpur to Agra with velocity $v$ in the positive $x$-direction.

The birth of the Kanpur baby is event $K$ with coordinates $(t_K, x_K) = (0, 0)$.

The birth of the Agra baby is event $A$ with coordinates $(t_A, x_A) = (0, L)$.

Using the Lorentz transformation for time, $t' = \gamma \left( t - $\dfrac{vx}{c^2} \right).

The time of birth of the Kanpur baby in the train frame is $t'_K = \gamma \left( 0 - $\dfrac{v(0)}{c^2} \right) =$0$.

The time of birth of the Agra baby in the train frame is $t'_A = \gamma \left( 0 - $\dfrac{vL}{c^2} \right) = -\dfrac{\gamma vL}{c^2}.

Since $t'_A < t'_K$, the Agra baby is born earlier in the train frame.

Therefore, the Agra baby is elder in the reference frame of the train.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: According to the station clocks, two babies are born at the exact same instant, one in Kanpur and the other in Agra. Who is elder in the reference frame of the 12034 Shatabdi Express travelling from Agra to Kanpur?
options: Both babies are of the exact same age
It depends on the exact speed of the train
questions.solution:
Let the ground frame be $S$ and the train frame be $S'$.

Let Agra be at the origin $x = 0$ and Kanpur be at $x = L$, where $L > 0$.

The train is travelling from Agra to Kanpur, so its velocity $v$ is in the positive $x$-direction.

The two births are simultaneous in the ground frame, so $t_A = t_K = 0$.

Using the Lorentz transformation for time, $t' = \gamma \left( t - $\dfrac{vx}{c^2} \right).

For the baby born in Agra: $t'_A = \gamma \left( 0 - $\dfrac{v(0)}{c^2} \right) =$0$.

For the baby born in Kanpur: $t'_K = \gamma \left( 0 - $\dfrac{vL}{c^2} \right) = -\dfrac{\gamma vL}{c^2}.

Since $v > 0$ and $L > 0$, we have $t'_K < t'_A$.

This means that in the train's reference frame, the baby in Kanpur was born earlier than the baby in Agra. Therefore, the Kanpur baby is elder.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two babies are born on a moving train; one is in the compartment adjacent to the engine and the other is in the compartment adjacent to the guard. According to the train frame, the babies are born at the exact same instant of time. Who is elder according to the ground frame?
options: Both babies are exactly the same age
The baby adjacent to the engine
The baby adjacent to the guard
It depends on the magnitude of the train's speed
questions.solution:
Let the train frame be $S'$ moving with velocity $v$ relative to the ground frame $S$ in the positive $x$-direction.

Let the position of the compartment adjacent to the guard (rear of the train) be $x'_{1} = 0$ and the compartment adjacent to the engine (front of the train) be $x'_{2} = L$, where $L$ is the proper length of the train.

According to the train frame, the babies are born at the exact same instant, so $t'_{1} = t'_{2} = 0$.

Using the Lorentz transformation for time, the time of an event in the ground frame is given by:
$t = \gamma \left(t' + $\dfrac{v x'}{c^2}\right)

For the baby born adjacent to the guard:
$t_{1} = \gamma \left(0 + 0\right) = 0$

For the baby born adjacent to the engine:
$t_{2} = \gamma \left(0 + $\dfrac{v L}{c^2}\right) = \dfrac{\gamma v L}{c^2}

Since $t_{2} > t_{1}$, the birth of the baby adjacent to the engine occurs later in the ground frame.

Because the baby adjacent to the guard is born earlier in the ground frame, this baby is elder according to the observers on the ground.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Assume that Devlok (heaven) moves constantly at a speed of $0.9999c$ relative to the earth. In the earth's frame of reference, how much time elapses on the earth for one day to pass on Devlok?
questions.solution:
The time dilation formula is given by $\Delta t = \dfrac{\Delta t_0}{\sqrt{1 - \dfrac{v^2}{c^2}}}$

Here, the proper time $\Delta t_0 = 1$ day and the velocity $v = 0.9999c$.

Calculating the term inside the square root:

$1 - \dfrac{v^2}{c^2} = (1 - 0.9999)(1 + 0.9999) = 0.0001 \times 1.9999 \approx 2 \times 10^{-4}$

Taking the square root:

$\sqrt{1 - \dfrac{v^2}{c^2}} \approx \sqrt{2 \times 10^{-4}} = 1.414 \times 10^{-2}$

Substituting this back into the time dilation formula:

$\Delta t = \dfrac{1}{1.414 \times 10^{-2}} = \dfrac{100}{1.414} = 70.7$ days

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If a person lives on average $100$ years in his rest frame, determine how long he lives in the earth frame if he spends his entire life on a spaceship travelling at $60\%$ of the speed of light.
questions.solution:
The proper time interval, which is the lifetime measured in the person's rest frame, is $\Delta t_0 = 100$ years.

The velocity of the spaceship relative to the Earth frame is $v = 0.6c$.

Using the time dilation formula, the lifetime measured in the Earth frame is given by:

$\Delta t = \dfrac{\Delta t_0}{\sqrt{1 - \dfrac{v^2}{c^2}}}$

Substituting the given values:

$\Delta t = \dfrac{100}{\sqrt{1 - (0.6)^2}}$

$\Delta t = \dfrac{100}{\sqrt{1 - 0.36}}$

$\Delta t = \dfrac{100}{\sqrt{0.64}}$

$\Delta t = \dfrac{100}{0.8} = 125 \text{ years}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An electric bulb, linked to a make and break power supply, turns off and on every second in its rest frame. Determine the frequency of its switching off and on as observed from a spaceship travelling at a speed of $0.8c$.
questions.solution:
The proper time interval between two consecutive switching events in the rest frame of the bulb is $\Delta t_0 = 1 \text{ s}$.

The spaceship is moving with a speed $v = 0.8c$ relative to the bulb.

According to the time dilation formula, the time interval $\Delta t$ observed from the spaceship is given by:

$\Delta t = \dfrac{\Delta t_0}{\sqrt{1 - \dfrac{v^2}{c^2}}}$

Substituting $v = 0.8c$ and $\Delta t_0 = 1 \text{ s}$:

$\Delta t = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - (0.8)^2}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - 0.64}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{0.36}} = \dfrac{1}{0.6} \text{ s}$

The observed frequency $f$ is the reciprocal of the observed time interval:

$f = \dfrac{1}{\Delta t} = 0.6 \text{ Hz}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A person travelling in a car moving at $100 \text{ km h}^{-1}$ observes that his wristwatch agrees with the clock on a tower $A$. When the car reaches another tower $B$, $1000 \text{ km}$ (in the earth's frame) from the tower $A$, by what amount will his wristwatch lag or lead the clock on tower $B$?
questions.solution:
The time taken by the car to travel from tower $A$ to tower $B$ in the Earth's frame is given by $t = \dfrac{d}{v}$.

Substituting $d = 1000 \text{ km}$ and $v = 100 \text{ km h}^{-1}$, we get $t = \dfrac{1000}{100} = 10 \text{ h} = 36000 \text{ s}$.

The speed of the car in $\text{m s}^{-1}$ is $v = 100 \times \dfrac{5}{18} = \dfrac{250}{9} \text{ m s}^{-1}$.

According to the time dilation formula, the proper time $t_0$ measured by the wristwatch in the car is related to the time $t$ in the Earth's frame by $t_0 = t \sqrt{1 - \dfrac{v^2}{c^2}}$.

Since $v \ll c$, using the binomial expansion, we can approximate this as $t_0 \approx t \left(1 - $\dfrac{v^2}{2c^2}\right).

The time difference between the clock on tower $B$ and the wristwatch is $\Delta t = t - t_0 = t $\dfrac{v^2}{2c^2}.

Substituting the values, we get $\Delta t = 36000 \times $\dfrac{1}{2} \times \left(\dfrac{250}{9 \times 3 \times 10^8}\right)^2$.

$\Delta t = 18000 \times \$left(\dfrac{25}{27 \times 10^7}\right)^2 = 18000 \times $\dfrac{625}{729 \times 10^{14}} = \dfrac{11250000}{729 \times 10^{14}} \text{ s}.

$\Delta t = $\dfrac{1125}{729} \times$10^{-10} \text{ s} \approx 1.543 \times 10^{-10} \text{ s} = 0.154 \text{ ns}$.

Since $t_0 < t$, the wristwatch shows less time than the clock on tower $B$. Therefore, the wristwatch lags the clock on tower $B$ by $0.154 \text{ ns}$.$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Determine the speed at which the volume of an object shrinks to half of its rest value.
questions.solution:
Let the rest volume of the object be $V_0 = L_x L_y L_z$.

When the object moves with a speed $v$ along the x-axis, its length in the direction of motion contracts due to length contraction, while the perpendicular dimensions remain unchanged.

The new length is $L'_x = L_x \sqrt{1 - \dfrac{v^2}{c^2}}$.

The new volume is $V = L'_x L_y L_z = V_0 \sqrt{1 - \dfrac{v^2}{c^2}}$.

Given that the volume shrinks to half of its rest value, $V = \dfrac{V_0}{2}$.

$\dfrac{V_0}{2} = V_0 \sqrt{1 - \dfrac{v^2}{c^2}}$

$\dfrac{1}{4} = 1 - \dfrac{v^2}{c^2}$

$\dfrac{v^2}{c^2} = \dfrac{3}{4}$

$v = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}\,c}{2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Before decaying, a specific particle produced in a nuclear reactor leaves a $1 \text{ cm}$ track. Determine the life of the particle in the lab frame, assuming it travelled at $0.995c$.
questions.solution:
Distance travelled by the particle in the lab frame, $d = 1 \text{ cm} = 10^{-2} \text{ m}$

Speed of the particle, $v = 0.995c = 0.995 \times 3 \times 10^8 \text{ m/s} = 2.985 \times 10^8 \text{ m/s}$

The life of the particle in the lab frame is the time taken to travel this distance:

$t = \dfrac{d}{v}$

$t = \dfrac{10^{-2}}{2.985 \times 10^8} \text{ s}$

$t \approx 3.35 \times 10^{-11} \text{ s}$

$t = 33.5 \times 10^{-12} \text{ s} = 33.5 \text{ ps}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Before decaying, a specific particle produced in a nuclear reactor leaves a $1 \text{ cm}$ track. Determine the life of the particle in the frame of the particle, assuming it travelled at $0.995c$.
questions.solution:
The distance travelled by the particle in the laboratory frame is $L = 1 \text{ cm} = 10^{-2} \text{ m}$.

The speed of the particle is $v = 0.995c$.

The time lived by the particle in the laboratory frame is given by:

$\Delta t = \dfrac{L}{v} = \dfrac{10^{-2}}{0.995 \times 3 \times 10^8} = \dfrac{10^{-10}}{2.985} \approx 33.5 \times 10^{-12} \text{ s}$

The life of the particle in its own rest frame (proper time $\Delta t_0$) is related to the laboratory time by time dilation:

$\Delta t = \dfrac{\Delta t_0}{\sqrt{1 - \dfrac{v^2}{c^2}}}$

$\Rightarrow \Delta t_0 = \Delta t \sqrt{1 - \dfrac{v^2}{c^2}}$

Substituting the values:

$\Delta t_0 = 33.5 \times 10^{-12} \times \sqrt{1 - (0.995)^2}$

$\Delta t_0 = 33.5 \times 10^{-12} \times \sqrt{1 - 0.990025}$

$\Delta t_0 = 33.5 \times 10^{-12} \times \sqrt{0.009975}$

$\Delta t_0 \approx 33.5 \times 10^{-12} \times 0.09987$

$\Delta t_0 \approx 3.35 \times 10^{-12} \text{ s} = 3.35 \text{ ps}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Determine the fractional change in the mass of a spring upon being compressed by $1 \text{ cm}$. At its natural length, the spring has a mass of $200 \text{ g}$ and a spring constant of $500 \text{ N m}^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
Energy stored in the spring is given by $U = \dfrac{1}{2}kx^2$.

Substituting the given values:

$U = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 500 \times (0.01)^2 = 0.025 \text{ J}$

By mass-energy equivalence, the change in mass is $\Delta m = \dfrac{U}{c^2}$.

The fractional change in mass is $\dfrac{\Delta m}{m} = \dfrac{U}{mc^2}$.

Substituting the values:

$\dfrac{\Delta m}{m} = \dfrac{0.025}{0.2 \times (3 \times 10^8)^2}$

$\dfrac{\Delta m}{m} = \dfrac{0.025}{0.2 \times 9 \times 10^{16}} = \dfrac{0.025}{1.8 \times 10^{16}}$

$\dfrac{\Delta m}{m} = \dfrac{2.5}{1.8} \times 10^{-18} \approx 1.388 \times 10^{-18} \approx 1.4 \times 10^{-18}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Determine the increase in mass when $1 \text{ kg}$ of water is heated from $0^{}^{{}^{\circ}} \text{C}$ to $100^{}^{{}^{\circ}} \text{C}$. The specific heat capacity of water is given as $4200 \text{ J kg}^{-1} \textK^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
The heat energy required to raise the temperature of water is given by $\Delta Q = mc\Delta T$.

Substituting the given values:

$\Delta Q = 1 \times 4200 \times 100 = 4.2 \times 10^5 \text{ J}$

According to Einstein's mass-energy equivalence principle, $\Delta E = \Delta m c^2$. Since the heat supplied increases the internal energy of the water, $\Delta E = \Delta Q$.

Therefore, the increase in mass is:

$\Delta m = \dfrac{\Delta Q}{c^2}$

Substituting the values of $\Delta Q$ and the speed of light $c = 3 \times 10^8 \text{ m s}^{-1}$:

$\Delta m = \dfrac{4.2 \times 10^5}{(3 \times 10^8)^2} = \dfrac{4.2 \times 10^5}{9 \times 10^{16}}$

$\Delta m = 0.466 \times 10^{-11} \text{ kg} \approx 4.7 \times 10^{-12} \text{ kg}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Determine the loss in the mass of $1 \text{ mole}$ of an ideal monatomic gas held in a rigid container as it cools down by $10^{}^{{}^{\circ}} \text{C}$. The gas constant is given as $R = 8.3 \text{ J K}^{-1} \text{mol}^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
The change in internal energy of the gas during cooling at constant volume is given by $\Delta U = n C_v \Delta T$.

For a monatomic gas, $C_v = \dfrac{3}{2} R$.

Substituting the given values, $n = 1 \text{ mole}$, $R = 8.3 \text{ J K}^{-1} \text{mol}^{-1}$, and $\Delta T = 10 \text{ K}$:

$\Delta U = 1 \times \dfrac{3}{2} \times 8.3 \times 10 = 124.5 \text{ J}$

According to the mass-energy equivalence principle, the loss in mass is $\Delta m = \dfrac{\Delta U}{c^2}$.

Using $c = 3 \times 10^8 \text{ m s}^{-1}$:

$\Delta m = \dfrac{124.5}{(3 \times 10^8)^2} = \dfrac{124.5}{9 \times 10^{16}} = 13.83 \times 10^{-16} \text{ kg}$

$\Delta m \approx 1.38 \times 10^{-15} \text{ kg}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: When a boy starts running at a speed of $12 \text{ km h}^{-1}$, by what fraction does his mass increase?
questions.solution:
Speed $v = 12 \text{ km h}^{-1} = 12 \times \dfrac{5}{18} \text{ m s}^{-1} = \dfrac{10}{3} \text{ m s}^{-1}$

The relativistic mass is given by $m = \dfrac{m_0}{\sqrt{1 - \dfrac{v^2}{c^2}}}$

The fractional increase in mass is $\dfrac{\Delta m}{m_0} = \dfrac{m - m_0}{m_0} = \left(1 - \dfrac{v^2}{c^2}\right)^{-1/2} - 1$

Since $v \ll c$, using the binomial expansion:

$\dfrac{\Delta m}{m_0} \approx \left(1 + \dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{v^2}{c^2}\right) - 1 = \dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{v^2}{c^2}$

Substituting the values:

$\dfrac{\Delta m}{m_0} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{10}{3}\right)^2}{(3 \times 10^8)^2}$

$\dfrac{\Delta m}{m_0} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{100}{9 \times 9 \times 10^{16}} = \dfrac{100}{162 \times 10^{16}}$

$\dfrac{\Delta m}{m_0} = \dfrac{1}{1.62} \times 10^{-16} \approx 6.17 \times 10^{-17}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Suspended from a sensitive balance is a $100 \text{ W}$ bulb along with its power supply. Determine the change in the recorded mass after the bulb is kept on for $1 \text{ year}$.
questions.solution:
The energy radiated by the bulb in one year is given by $E = P \times t$.

Substituting the given values:

$P = 100 \text{ W}$

$t = 1 \text{ year} = 365 \times 24 \times 60 \times 60 \text{ s} = 3.1536 \times 10^7 \text{ s}$

$E = 100 \times 3.1536 \times 10^7 = 3.1536 \times 10^9 \text{ J}$

According to the mass-energy equivalence principle, the energy leaving the system as light and heat results in a decrease in the mass of the system.

$\Delta m = \dfrac{E}{c^2}$

$\Delta m = \dfrac{3.1536 \times 10^9}{(3 \times 10^8)^2}$

$\Delta m = \dfrac{3.1536 \times 10^9}{9 \times 10^{16}}$

$\Delta m = 0.3504 \times 10^{-7} \text{ kg} \approx 3.5 \times 10^{-8} \text{ kg}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Just outside the earth's atmosphere, energy from the sun arrives at a rate of $1400 \text{ W m}^{-2}$. The distance separating the sun and the earth is $1.5 \times 10^{11} \text{ m}$. Determine the rate at which the sun is losing its mass.
questions.solution:
The intensity of solar radiation at the earth's distance is $I = 1400 \text{ W m}^{-2}$.

The total power radiated by the sun is distributed over a spherical surface of radius $R = 1.5 \times 10^{11} \text{ m}$.

Total power $P = I \times 4\pi R^2$

Substituting the given values:

$P = 1400 \times 4\pi \times (1.5 \times 10^{11})^2$

$P = 1400 \times 4\pi \times 2.25 \times 10^{22} = 12600\pi \times 10^{22} \text{ J s}^{-1}$

According to the mass-energy equivalence principle, $E = mc^2$, the rate of mass loss is:

$\dfrac{dm}{dt} = \dfrac{P}{c^2}$

Using $c = 3 \times 10^8 \text{ m s}^{-1}$:

$\dfrac{dm}{dt} = \dfrac{12600\pi \times 10^{22}}{(3 \times 10^8)^2}$

$\dfrac{dm}{dt} = \dfrac{12600\pi \times 10^{22}}{9 \times 10^{16}} = 1400\pi \times 10^6 \text{ kg s}^{-1}$

Taking $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$:

$\dfrac{dm}{dt} = 1400 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 10^6 = 200 \times 22 \times 10^6 = 4400 \times 10^6 \text{ kg s}^{-1}$

$\dfrac{dm}{dt} = 4.4 \times 10^9 \text{ kg s}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Just outside the earth's atmosphere, energy from the sun arrives at a rate of $1400 \text{ W m}^{-2}$. The distance separating the sun and the earth is $1.5 \times 10^{11} \text{ m}$. If the present mass of the sun is $2 \times 10^{30} \text{ kg}$, determine how long the sun will last assuming a constant decay at this rate.
questions.solution:
Total power radiated by the sun is given by $P = S \times 4\pi R^2$, where $S$ is the solar constant and $R$ is the distance between the sun and the earth.

$P = 1400 \times 4\pi \times (1.5 \times 10^{11})^2$

$P = 1400 \times 4\pi \times 2.25 \times 10^{22} = 1.26\pi \times 10^{26} \text{ W}$

The rate of mass decay of the sun is obtained using Einstein's mass-energy equivalence, $\dfrac{dm}{dt} = \dfrac{P}{c^2}$.

$\dfrac{dm}{dt} = \dfrac{1.26\pi \times 10^{26}}{(3 \times 10^8)^2} = \dfrac{1.26\pi \times 10^{26}}{9 \times 10^{16}} = 1.4\pi \times 10^9 \text{ kg s}^{-1}$

The time the sun will last is $t = \dfrac{M}{dm/dt}$, where $M$ is the present mass of the sun.

$t = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{30}}{1.4\pi \times 10^9} = \dfrac{1}{0.7\pi} \times 10^{21} \text{ s} \approx 4.55 \times 10^{20} \text{ s}$

Converting the time from seconds to years using $1 \text{ y} \approx 3.15 \times 10^7 \text{ s}$:

$t = \dfrac{4.55 \times 10^{20}}{3.15 \times 10^7} \text{ y} \approx 1.44 \times 10^{13} \text{ y}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An electron and a positron travelling at small speeds collide and annihilate each other. Determine the energy of the resulting gamma photon.
questions.solution:
The annihilation of an electron and a positron at small speeds (negligible kinetic energy) produces two gamma photons to conserve linear momentum. The initial momentum is approximately zero, so the two photons must travel in opposite directions with equal momenta, and therefore equal energies.

The total initial energy of the system is the sum of the rest mass energies of the electron and the positron:

$E_{\text{initial}} = m_e c^2 + m_e c^2 = 2m_e c^2$

The rest mass energy of an electron (or positron) is:

$m_e c^2 = 0.51 \text{ MeV}$

Total initial energy $= 2 \times 0.51 \text{ MeV} = 1.02 \text{ MeV}$

By conservation of energy, the sum of the energies of the two gamma photons must equal the total initial energy:

$2E_{\gamma} = 1.02 \text{ MeV}$

$E_{\gamma} = \dfrac{1.02 \text{ MeV}}{2} = 0.51 \text{ MeV}$

Thus, the energy of each resulting gamma photon is $0.51 \text{ MeV}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Determine the mass, the kinetic energy, and the momentum of an electron travelling at $0.8c$.
questions.solution:
The rest mass of an electron is $m_0 = 9.1 \times 10^{-31} \text{ kg}$.

The relativistic factor $\gamma$ is given by:

$\gamma = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - \dfrac{v^2}{c^2}}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - (0.8)^2}} = \dfrac{1}{0.6} = \dfrac{5}{3}$

The relativistic mass $m$ is:

$m = \gamma m_0 = \dfrac{5}{3} \times 9.1 \times 10^{-31} \text{ kg} \approx 15.2 \times 10^{-31} \text{ kg}$

The kinetic energy $K$ is:

$K = (\gamma - 1)m_0 c^2 = \left(\dfrac{5}{3} - 1\right) \times 9.1 \times 10^{-31} \times (3 \times 10^8)^2$

$K = \dfrac{2}{3} \times 9.1 \times 10^{-31} \times 9 \times 10^{16} = 54.6 \times 10^{-15} \text{ J} \approx 5.5 \times 10^{-14} \text{ J}$

The momentum $p$ is:

$p = mv = \left(\dfrac{5}{3} \times 9.1 \times 10^{-31}\right) \times (0.8 \times 3 \times 10^8)$

$p = 36.4 \times 10^{-23} \text{ kg m s}^{-1} \approx 3.65 \times 10^{-22} \text{ kg m s}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Through what potential difference must an electron be accelerated to give it a speed of $0.6c$?
questions.solution:
The speed of the electron is $v = 0.6c$, which is comparable to the speed of light, so relativistic mechanics must be used.

The relativistic kinetic energy $K$ of the electron is given by $K = (\gamma - 1)m_0 c^2$, where $\gamma = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - \dfrac{v^2}{c^2}}}$.

Substituting $v = 0.6c$:

$\gamma = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - (0.6)^2}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - 0.36}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{0.64}} = \dfrac{1}{0.8} = 1.25$

The kinetic energy gained by the electron is:

$K = (1.25 - 1)m_0 c^2 = 0.25 m_0 c^2$

The rest mass energy of an electron is $m_0 c^2 \approx 511 \text{ keV}$.

$K = 0.25 \times 511 \text{ keV} = 127.75 \text{ keV} \approx 128 \text{ keV}$

Since the kinetic energy gained by accelerating an electron through a potential difference $V$ is $K = eV$, we get:

$eV = 128 \text{ keV} \Rightarrow V = 128 \text{ kV}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Through what potential difference must an electron be accelerated to give it a speed of $0.9c$?
questions.solution:
The speed of the electron is $v = 0.9c$, which is comparable to the speed of light, so relativistic mechanics must be used.

The relativistic factor $\gamma$ is given by:
$\gamma = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - \dfrac{v^2}{c^2}}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - 0.81}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{0.19}} \approx 2.294$

The kinetic energy $K$ of the electron is:
$K = (\gamma - 1)m_0 c^2$

Using the rest mass energy of an electron, $m_0 c^2 \approx 0.511 \text{ MeV}$:
$K = (2.294 - 1) \times 0.511 \text{ MeV} = 1.294 \times 0.511 \text{ MeV} \approx 0.661 \text{ MeV} = 661 \text{ keV}$

Since the kinetic energy is gained by accelerating the electron through a potential difference $V$, we have $K = eV$.

$V = \dfrac{661 \text{ keV}}{e} = 661 \text{ kV}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Determine the speed of an electron possessing a kinetic energy of $1 \text{ eV}$.
questions.solution:
The kinetic energy of the electron is given as $K = 1 \text{ eV}$.

Converting to Joules:

$K = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J}$

The mass of an electron is $m = 9.1 \times 10^{-31} \text{ kg}$.

Using the formula for kinetic energy $K = \dfrac{1}{2} m v^2$, the speed $v$ is:

$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2K}{m}}$

Substituting the values:

$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}}{9.1 \times 10^{-31}}}$

$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{3.2}{9.1} \times 10^{12}}$

$v = \sqrt{0.3516 \times 10^{12}}$

$v \approx 0.593 \times 10^{6} \text{ m s}^{-1} = 5.93 \times 10^{5} \text{ m s}^{-1}$

The closest value among the options is $5.92 \times 10^{5} \text{ m s}^{-1}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Find the speed of an electron that has a kinetic energy of $10 \text{ MeV}$.
questions.solution:
The rest mass energy of an electron is $E_0 = m_0 c^2 = 0.511 \text{ MeV}$.

The kinetic energy is $K = 10 \text{ MeV}$.

The total energy of the electron is given by $E = K + E_0 = 10 + 0.511 = 10.511 \text{ MeV}$.

Using the relativistic energy relation $E = \dfrac{m_0 c^2}{\sqrt{1 - \dfrac{v^2}{c^2}}}$, we get:

$10.511 = \dfrac{0.511}{\sqrt{1 - \dfrac{v^2}{c^2}}}$

$\sqrt{1 - \dfrac{v^2}{c^2}} = \dfrac{0.511}{10.511} \approx 0.0486$

Squaring both sides:

$1 - \dfrac{v^2}{c^2} \approx (0.0486)^2 \approx 0.00236$

$\dfrac{v^2}{c^2} \approx 1 - 0.00236 = 0.99764$

$\dfrac{v}{c} \approx \sqrt{0.99764} \approx 0.9988$

Taking $c = 3 \times 10^8 \text{ m s}^{-1}$:

$v \approx 0.9988 \times 3 \times 10^8 \text{ m s}^{-1} = 2.996 \times 10^8 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Through what potential difference must an electron be accelerated to give it a speed of $0.99c$?
questions.solution:
The rest mass energy of an electron is $m_0 c^2 = 0.511 \text{ MeV}$.

The kinetic energy of a relativistic particle is given by $K = (\gamma - 1)m_0 c^2$, where $\gamma = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - \dfrac{v^2}{c^2}}}$.

Given $v = 0.99c$, we calculate $\gamma$ as:

$\gamma = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - (0.99)^2}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - 0.9801}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{0.0199}} \approx 7.089$

The kinetic energy is:

$K = (7.089 - 1) \times 0.511 \text{ MeV} = 6.089 \times 0.511 \text{ MeV} \approx 3.11 \text{ MeV}$

Since the kinetic energy is gained by accelerating the electron through a potential difference $V$, we have $K = eV$.

$eV = 3.11 \text{ MeV} \Rightarrow V = 3.1 \text{ MV}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Calculate the speed of an electron whose kinetic energy is $10 \text{ keV}$.
questions.solution:
Given:
Kinetic energy of the electron, $K = 10 \text{ keV} = 10 \times 10^3 \text{ eV}$

Converting kinetic energy into Joules:
$K = 10^4 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J} = 1.6 \times 10^{-15} \text{ J}$

Mass of an electron, $m = 9.1 \times 10^{-31} \text{ kg}$

Using the non-relativistic formula for kinetic energy:
$K = \dfrac{1}{2} m v^2$

Rearranging for speed $v$:
$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2K}{m}}$

Substituting the values:
$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-15}}{9.1 \times 10^{-31}}}$

$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{3.2 \times 10^{-15}}{9.1 \times 10^{-31}}}$

$v = \sqrt{0.3516 \times 10^{16}}$

$v \approx 5.93 \times 10^7 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

Answer: $5.93 \times 10^{7} \text{ m s}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Calculate the kinetic energy, in electronvolts, of an electron that has a mass equal to twice its rest mass.
questions.solution:
Total energy of a relativistic particle is given by $E = mc^2$.

Given that the mass of the electron is twice its rest mass, $m = 2m_0$.

Total energy $E = 2m_0c^2$.

Kinetic energy $K$ is the difference between the total energy and the rest mass energy:

$K = E - m_0c^2$

$K = 2m_0c^2 - m_0c^2 = m_0c^2$

The rest mass energy of an electron is $m_0c^2 \approx 0.511 \text{ MeV} = 511 \times 10^3 \text{ eV}$.

Therefore, the kinetic energy of the electron is $511 \times 10^3 \text{ eV}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Determine the speed at which the kinetic energy of a particle will deviate by $1\%$ from its nonrelativistic value $\dfrac{1}{2} m_0 v^2$.
questions.solution:
The relativistic kinetic energy is given by $K = m_0 c^2 (\gamma - 1) = m_0 c^2 \left( $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - \dfrac{v^2}{c^2}}} -$1 \right)$.

Using the binomial expansion for $v \ll c$, we get:

$K = m_0 c² \left(1 + \dfrac{1}{2} \dfrac{v^2}{c^2} + \dfrac{3}{8} \dfrac{v^4}{c^4} + \dots -1 \right)$

$K \approx \dfrac{1}{2}m_0 v² + \dfrac{3}{8}m_0 \dfrac{v^4}{c^2}$

The nonrelativistic kinetic energy is $K_{nr} = \dfrac{1}{2}m_0 v²$.

The fractional deviation is given by:

$\dfrac{K - K_{nr}}{K_{nr}} = \dfrac{\dfrac{3}{8} m_0 \dfrac{v^4}{c^2}}{\dfrac{1}{2} m_0 v^2} = \dfrac{3}{4} \dfrac{v^2}{c^2}$

Given that the deviation is $1\% = 0.01$:

$\dfrac{3}{4} \dfrac{v^2}{c^2} =0.01$

$v^2 = \dfrac{0.04}{3}c^2$

$v = \dfrac{0.2}{\sqrt{3}}c$

Substituting $c = 3 \times10^8 \text{ m/s}$:

$v = \dfrac{0.2}{\sqrt{3}} \times3 \times10^8 = 0.2 \times \sqrt{3} \times10^8$

$v \approx0.2 \times1.732 \times10^8 = 3.464 \times10^7 \text{ m/s}$
